Wirehaired Pointing Griffon: Coat, Energy, and Family Fit

A grounded guide to the Wirehaired Pointing Griffon: its wiry coat and hand-stripping, high exercise needs, family fit, and a cost plan built on local quotes.

Published: 2026-10-26Sources checked: 3Educational planning guide

The Wirehaired Pointing Griffon is a versatile, close-working gundog whose defining planning points are a weatherproof wiry coat, a genuine need for daily activity and a job, and a friendly temperament that fits active families.

A close-working, versatile gundog

Developed in the Netherlands in the 1800s by Edward Korthals, the Wirehaired Pointing Griffon was bred as a hardy, versatile hunter, which is why it is also known as the Korthals Griffon, according to VCA Animal Hospitals. VCA notes the breed tends to work close to the handler rather than ranging widely, which makes it agreeable company on a walk as well as in the field. It describes a medium dog standing about 20 to 24 inches, weighing 50 to 60 pounds, with a life expectancy of roughly 10 to 12 years.

Temperament, per VCA, is friendly, intelligent, and energetic, eager to please and a fast learner, though sometimes aloof with strangers and excellent with children. VCA says most Griffons fit well into households with other friendly dogs but will not back down from a challenge, and that cats may prove too tempting for a dog that loves a boisterous romp. This is a people-oriented working dog, not an ornament, and it thrives when included in family life.

VCA frames the ideal owner as active and outdoorsy, with a fenced yard or access to one, and notes that experience is preferred though the breed's eagerness to please makes training rewarding. The single biggest fit question is not friendliness but whether your lifestyle can supply enough activity and mental work.

Understanding the wiry coat

VCA calls the Griffon an easy-care pet that needs only weekly brushing, with the bonus of minimal shedding. The wiry, weather-resistant topcoat, usually chestnut and white and often with roaning, is part of what makes the breed hardy across terrain and seasons. Two caveats matter: owners who show their dogs do some trimming or hand-stripping around the head and feet, and the beard needs frequent cleaning because it catches crumbs and water, and, as VCA wryly notes, the breed likes to dry a dripping beard on clean clothing. VCA also observes the wiry coat tends to carry bits of the outdoors inside.

Hand-stripping is worth understanding before you commit. Unlike clipping, it removes dead hairs to maintain the harsh texture that protects the dog, and it takes time and skill. Many pet owners simply keep the coat tidy with weekly brushing and occasional tidying, while show homes invest more. Decide which camp you are in, because it changes both your time and your grooming budget.

If you plan to show or prefer a tidy coat, budget for hand-stripping time or a groomer who offers it; our hand-stripping cost guide explains why this service differs from clipping, and the grooming salon interview helps you find the right provider.

Exercise and the need for a job

VCA rates the Griffon's exercise needs as high, requiring a daily walk plus running and play, and lists "needs a job" among the breed's defining challenges. Left without an outlet, an intelligent sporting dog often invents its own entertainment, which can look like chewing, digging, or restlessness. Plan for real daily activity and structured mental work such as tracking, fetch games, hunt tests, or agility, all of which VCA says the breed can enjoy and compete in.

The good news is that VCA describes the breed as fine home alone with plenty of exercise first, so a tired Griffon can settle while you work. The catch is the word "first": the exercise has to happen, rain or shine, before the dog is expected to relax. That is a real time commitment, most days, for the life of the dog. This breed is a close cousin in energy to other versatile gundogs, so if you are weighing options, compare with a pointer using our German Shorthaired Pointer exercise guide.

For pacing daily activity, see the exercise time budget and the hiking breed checklist. If your week has little room for movement, compare with a lower-drive breed using working-dog lifestyle mismatch.

Cost worksheet for an active sporting dog

Costs here center on activity, coat, and preventive health rather than sheer size. Fill each line with quotes from your area.

LineFormula to fill with local quotes
Setupcrate + bed + long leash + brush + initial veterinary exam quote
Monthly food(measured daily portion for a 50-60 lb active dog x cost per unit) x 30
Monthly routineparasite prevention + training treats + occasional beard/ear cleaning supplies
Annual care(monthly food + monthly routine) x 12 + wellness exam + vaccine quote + hand-stripping sessions x price per visit (if used)
Reservefund for orthopedic or eye care; ask your clinic for a written estimate

Move the annual line into the five-year cost framework and size the buffer with the emergency fund formula. Remember that a working dog's costs are as much about time as money: the daily exercise, training, and grooming hours are real, even if they never appear on a receipt.

If you decide to keep the coat in show condition, the hand-stripping line can become one of your larger recurring costs, since it is skilled, time-intensive work. Many pet owners avoid it entirely and simply brush weekly, which keeps this line near zero. Decide your grooming approach before you fill in the worksheet, because it swings the total meaningfully.

A weekend-and-weekday scenario test

Imagine a typical week. On weekdays you provide a brisk walk plus a game of fetch or a short training session, then a chew or puzzle while you work. Once a week you brush the wiry coat and clean the beard and ears. On the weekend you take a longer outing, a hike, a swim, or a hunt-test class, so the dog's working brain gets a real workout and settles happily afterward.

Now imagine a rainy week with no outdoor time. Could you still meet the exercise and mental-work needs indoors with training games, scent work, and stair or hallway play? If the honest answer is no for weeks at a stretch, this high-energy breed may not suit your routine. Also picture the beard: a Griffon that has just drunk water or splashed in a pond will carry that moisture to your lap and furniture, so a household that prizes a spotless, dry couch should factor that in.

Finally, test the social side. VCA notes Griffons can be aloof with strangers and may find cats too tempting to leave alone. If you have a cat or frequent unfamiliar visitors, plan introductions and management from day one rather than assuming it will sort itself out.

Questions for a breeder or vet

VCA advises that Griffons come from eye- and orthopedic-screened lines and notes that entropion or ectropion can occur, so it cautions against buying a pup that will suffer painful eyes. Using Cornell's puppy-selection guide, ask a breeder:

  • What hip, elbow, eye, and cardiac testing did the parents complete? Can I verify results on OFA?
  • Have any eye conditions appeared in your line?
  • How do you socialize and start training the puppies?

Ask your veterinarian how much daily exercise suits a growing pup and how to protect joints. Cornell's hip dysplasia page stresses healthy weight and careful feeding of large-breed puppies.

Common mistakes

  • Clipping the wiry coat by default. Show and coat quality often rely on hand-stripping; discuss with a groomer first.
  • Skipping beard care. The beard holds food and water and needs frequent cleaning.
  • Under-exercising. VCA rates needs as high and says the breed needs a job.
  • Ignoring eye screening. Ask about entropion and ectropion in the line.

What this guide cannot tell you

These traits describe the breed in general based on veterinary sources and cannot predict your individual dog's energy, coat, or health. This is not medical advice. Whether to hand-strip, how much a puppy should exercise, and how to handle any eye or joint concern should be settled with a groomer and a veterinarian who see your dog. Costs vary by location, so the worksheet relies on quotes you collect yourself.

FAQ

How much grooming does a Wirehaired Pointing Griffon need?
VCA describes the breed as easy-care, needing only weekly brushing with minimal shedding. The extra tasks are cleaning the beard, which catches food and water, and, for show dogs or a tidy look, occasional hand-stripping around the head and feet. If you want a clipped, salon-shaped coat, discuss it with a groomer first, because hand-stripping is a different service you can price with local quotes.
Is this breed good with children?
VCA rates the Wirehaired Pointing Griffon as excellent with kids and any age is listed as fine, describing a friendly, people-oriented temperament. It can be aloof with strangers. As with any dog, supervise interactions and teach children gentle handling. The bigger fit question for families is usually the breed's high exercise and need for a job, not its friendliness.
How much exercise is enough?
VCA rates exercise needs as high: a daily walk plus running and play, along with a job to keep the mind busy. In practice that means committing to real daily activity and some structured mental work such as fetch, tracking, or a beginner dog sport. If your schedule cannot reliably provide this, a lower-energy breed may be a better match for your household.
